opus-5.5.text:
Language is the medium through which we come to understand ourselves and each other. It shapes what we can see as a problem in the first place. Many forms of domination don't announce themselves through overt coercion; they work through categories, through what gets named and what stays unnamed. Think of how long it took to have a word like "sexual harassment." Before that term existed, people experienced something real and harmful, but they lacked a shared concept to articulate it, contest it, and organize around it. Once the language existed, a whole set of claims became sayable, and therefore actionable.

So if you care about emancipation, freeing people from relationships of unjustified power, you can't just look at laws or material arrangements. You also have to ask: what does our vocabulary make visible, and what does it obscure? Whose experiences are encoded in the default meanings of words, and whose are treated as deviations?

This has become more pressing with large language models. These systems are trained on enormous amounts of human text, so they inherit both the emancipatory and the oppressive features of our linguistic practices. They can reproduce stereotypes, flatten dialects, or treat one cultural perspective as neutral. And because they're deployed at scale, they don't just reflect language, they increasingly shape it. They help write emails, summarize news, and answer questions. That gives them real influence over what concepts circulate and how people frame their own situations.

So, for me, examining language is a precondition for any serious emancipatory project. It's where we notice injustices that haven't been named yet, and it's increasingly where new technologies either expand or narrow the space of what people are able to think and say about their own lives.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to the fact that language isn't a neutral medium. It's not just a window we look through at the world; it's partly constitutive of the world we're able to see. The concepts we have available to us shape what we can notice, what we can name as a problem, and what we can even imagine as an alternative.

So if you care about emancipation, in the fairly classical sense of people being freed from forms of domination or constraint they haven't chosen, then you have to ask: where does that constraint actually live? And a surprising amount of it lives in language. It lives in the categories we inherit, the descriptions that get treated as obvious, the terms that carry evaluative weight without announcing it. Think of how much work a word like "natural" does, or "merit," or "efficiency." Those aren't just labels. They're arguments that have been compressed into vocabulary, and once compressed they become very hard to contest, because contesting them sounds like contesting common sense.

There's a tradition here, obviously. Wittgenstein talks about being held captive by a picture, and part of what he means is that a form of words can hold us in place. Critical theorists made a related point about ideology: that the most effective forms of power are the ones that don't look like power, that just look like how things are described. And feminist philosophers like Miranda Fricker have shown how a person can be harmed simply by lacking the words to make their experience intelligible, to themselves or to others. The concept of sexual harassment is the standard example. Before that phrase existed, something was happening, but it couldn't be properly articulated, and so it couldn't be properly resisted.

And I think this takes on a new urgency now, because we're building systems whose whole function is to produce and shape language at scale. Large language models aren't just answering questions. They're participating in the ongoing negotiation over what counts as a reasonable thing to say, what framings are default, which concepts get reinforced and which quietly drop out. If those systems absorb and amplify the existing vocabulary uncritically, they can entrench the very pictures that hold people captive, and do it with enormous fluency and reach.

So for me, examining language isn't a detour from the practical work of emancipation. It's part of the terrain. You can't free people from constraints that remain invisible, and language is where a great many of those constraints hide.

astra-6.text:
Because language helps shape what we can see, what we take for granted, and what we regard as possible. It doesn’t simply describe social relationships; it can also reinforce them. The categories we use to describe people, for example, can make a particular hierarchy appear natural rather than something that was created and could be changed.

So if emancipation involves challenging relations of domination, we also have to examine the terms in which those relations are understood. Who gets to name an injustice? Whose experience is intelligible within the vocabulary we share? And whose experience gets dismissed because we don’t yet have adequate concepts for it?

That doesn’t mean changing language is sufficient. Material conditions and institutions matter enormously. But developing a language in which people can articulate their experiences and question inherited assumptions can be part of making collective change possible.

sol-6.1.text:
Because language doesn’t simply describe the world; it also shapes how we understand it, whose experiences we recognize, and what kinds of change we can imagine. The categories we inherit can carry assumptions about who has authority, whose interests matter, and what counts as normal. Those assumptions can make unequal social relations seem natural or inevitable.

So emancipation requires being able to question those terms, to ask whose perspective they express and what they leave out. It also requires space for people to articulate their experiences in their own terms. Examining language is part of opening up the possibility of thinking and acting differently.
